prompt: Does top-k filtering affect the reported probability of the chosen token?
title: Top-k Filtering and Token Probabilities
body:
When a language model generates text, it computes raw scores called logits for every vocabulary word. A softmax function turns these logits into a probability distribution over all choices.

Look at the full softmax series to see how the initial probabilities spread across five candidate words before any filtering happens.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full softmax and top-2 sampling","caption":"The kept tokens originally hold 70% of the probability. Divide each kept probability by that total.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["on","near","under","by","in"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[42,28,16,8,6]},{"label":"Top-2 renormalized","values":[60,40,0,0,0]}]}}
```

Applying top-k filtering sets the probabilities of all tokens outside the top $k$ choices to zero.

To ensure the remaining probabilities still sum to one, the system rescales the surviving values by dividing each by their sum.

Notice how the top-2 renormalized series scales up the surviving words while completely eliminating the others.

prompt: What does predicting the mean give as a regression baseline?
title: Regression baseline of the mean
body:
When building a regression model, we often start with a naive baseline to judge if our features actually help. A common choice is predicting the constant mean of all target values in the training set.

This trivial model minimizes squared error without needing any input features at all.

Look for the horizontal line in the plot representing this constant prediction value.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A constant mean baseline","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Sample","min":1,"max":5},"y":{"label":"Target","min":0,"max":6},"series":[{"label":"Targets","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1,"y":1},{"x":2,"y":4},{"x":3,"y":2},{"x":4,"y":5},{"x":5,"y":3}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Mean prediction of 3","axis":"y","value":3}]}}
```

Calculating this baseline requires taking the arithmetic average of the target vector $y$. For targets $y_i$, our prediction $\hat{y}$ is simply $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i$.

Any sophisticated machine learning model must beat the mean squared error of this constant predictor to justify its complexity.

body:
When building a regression model, we often start with a simple reference point called a baseline. This baseline ignores all features and always predicts the same single value for any input.

Look for the horizontal line in the plot below, which shows this constant prediction across all samples.

```rh-diagram

```

When we use the arithmetic mean of the target values as this constant, we minimize the total squared error. This gives us a rigorous floor for how poorly our actual features are allowed to perform.

Any useful machine learning model must beat the mean squared error of this simple baseline to prove its worth.
